name: Liam Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No worries. I'll be honest, I nearly didn't come, because I figured you were selling something. But if it's just talking, I can talk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper pit, second year now. Alarm goes at four, I'm on the bus by quarter to five, pre-start checks on the truck, then twelve hours going up and down the ramp between the shovel and the crusher. I like the quiet in the cab and the sun coming up over the pit wall, but I'm still slow on the tight corners and the trainer, Gaz, still rides with me some shifts. What wears me out is nights, and the radio chatter when you're tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Every year someone comes round with a new system that's meant to change everything, and the trucks still need a guy in the seat. I'd probably put a laughing face on the union group chat and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wouldn't change much for me, because the thing I worry about isn't the chatbot stuff anyway. It's the driverless trucks, and those are already running at the big iron ore pits. Even if AI is all hype, the company doesn't need hype to buy a truck with no cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, get my hours up, get signed off on nights without Gaz. I'd stay active in the union, go to the monthly meetings at the pub on Station Street, maybe put my hand up for the delegate thing next year. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff because there's nothing in it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of a knot in the background, because the one thing that could hurt me isn't going away just because the computers didn't get clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company doesn't need hype to buy a driverless truck. Has anyone at Red Hill actually talked about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was a rumour last Christmas that head office sent two engineers out to measure the ramps. Nobody'd confirm it. Gaz says they've been saying it for ten years and it never happens here because our pit's too steep and too old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you believe Gaz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to. Gaz has been there twenty-two years, so he's seen a lot of rumours die. But he's also two years off retiring, so it's easy for him to be relaxed about it.

S0.say: I'd say I told everyone the hype was overblown and the trucks still need a person in the seat. I'd put a laughing face in the union group chat and leave it there.
S0.think: Privately I don't think it changes my risk much, because the threat to my job was never the chatbots. It's driverless haul trucks, and those exist whether or not AI lives up to the hype.
S0.do: Keeps working towards being signed off on night shifts without a trainer. Keeps going to monthly union meetings and thinks about standing as a delegate next year, while avoiding AI tools.
S0.feel: Mostly settled, with a small knot of worry about driverless trucks that doesn't go away.
S0.quote: Even if AI is all hype, the company doesn't need hype to buy a truck with no cab.
S0.fieldNote: He split the question neatly: AI hype is one thing, driverless trucks are another, and only the second scares him. He leans on his trainer's long memory for comfort but noticed himself that Gaz is close to retiring. The union is already his main way of handling worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company owes us. If they bring in self-driving trucks they should keep us on, put us in the control room or on maintenance, not just hand out a few weeks' pay. That's what I'd say at the meeting, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one they'd cut. I'm junior, I'm still slow on the corners, and I've got secondary school and a truck ticket. Last in, first out, and I'm last in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd push the union to get a deal in writing about who goes and who stays before the trucks arrive. I'd put a bit more aside each fortnight, maybe 200 instead of 100, because I've only got about three months saved. Apart from that I'd sit tight and see what they actually do, because I'm not going to quit a good-paying job over a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for the roster to come out when you know someone's getting dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit tight. If the company offered to train you for the control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Sitting in a room in the city watching screens isn't why I took this job, and I'm useless with computers. I'd probably say yes because the alternative is nothing, but I wouldn't be first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in this picture, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners. The pit makes money hand over fist, and every truck they take off a worker goes straight to the shareholders. It's not the technology's fault, it's who gets to decide what it's for.

S1.say: I'd say the company owes its workers and should keep us on in the control room or maintenance if it brings in driverless trucks. I'd say it at the union meeting word for word.
S1.think: Privately I know I'd be the first cut, because I'm junior, slow on corners and only have a truck ticket. Last in, first out applies to me.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a written deal on who stays before automation arrives and doubles what he saves each fortnight from 100 to 200. Otherwise waits to see what the company does rather than leave.
S1.feel: Slightly sick, like waiting for a roster that will drop someone.
S1.quote: Last in, first out, and I'm last in.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is about fairness for everyone, but privately he has already put himself at the front of the cut list. He'd take control-room training only reluctantly. He blames the owners rather than the technology, which fits his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and the government has to step in now. Stop the layoffs, tax the robots, something. I'd be sharing every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'd be done in mining inside a year. Two years isn't enough time for anything, not for me, not for the union, not for the government. I'd be twenty-nine with a truck licence for trucks that drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut right back straight away: no new pickup, cancel the gym, stop eating at the pub after shift. I'd go to every union rally and I'd vote for whoever promised a wage guarantee. If I got laid off I'd go on whatever payment there was and probably move back into Mum's spare room for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Like the ground's going out from under the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there someone at home you'd have to tell? What would you say that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mel works at the pharmacy in town. I'd probably say we'll be fine, because that's what you say. Then I'd lie awake doing sums in my head about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all you'd retrain for, if you had two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone says retrain, but into what? If the robots do the hands-on stuff and the computers do the thinking stuff, I don't know what's left that I'm good at. That's the bit that keeps going round.

S2.say: I'd say this is what we warned about and the government has to step in now, stop the layoffs or tax the robots. I'd share every petition going.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd be out of mining within a year, because two years isn't enough time for anyone to plan. I'd be twenty-nine with a licence for trucks that drive themselves.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once by dropping the new pickup, the gym and pub meals. Goes to union rallies, votes for a wage guarantee and, if laid off, takes government support and moves into his mum's spare room.
S2.feel: Properly scared, as if the ground were going out from under him.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine with a truck licence for trucks that drive themselves.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his calm broke. He sees no retraining path at all because he believes both hands-on and thinking work would be gone. He would tell his partner it's fine and then lie awake doing rent sums, a clear gap between say and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really. The union needs to get organised now, while there's still time, and the government should be making plans for towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but not by as much as you'd think. Mining towns don't change fast, and I don't either. I think I'd still be driving right up until the day they parked my truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand as delegate this time, no question, and push for redundancy deals and retraining money to be locked in. I'd save harder, try to get to six months in the bank. I'd write to our local member, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired just thinking about it. Five years of watching it come is its own kind of bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years of watching it come is its own kind of bad. What would that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every new piece of kit on site, you'd be wondering if it's the one. You'd look at the new guys starting and think, why are they even bothering? That kind of thing eats at a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for work outside mining in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. The money's better here than anything else in town, and Mel and I want a deposit for a house. I'd hang on as long as the pay kept coming.

S3.say: I'd say the union needs to organise now while there's time and the government should plan for mining towns like ours. It's the same message as the fast picture, just with a deadline.
S3.think: Privately I think five years helps less than it sounds, because mining towns and I both change slowly. I'd probably keep driving until the day they parked my truck.
S3.do: Stands for union delegate and pushes for redundancy and retraining money to be locked in. Saves towards six months of expenses and writes to the local member of parliament for the first time.
S3.feel: Tired and worn down at the thought of five years of watching it approach.
S3.quote: You'd look at the new guys starting and think, why are they even bothering?
S3.fieldNote: Extra time made him more organised politically but not more willing to change his own path. He described the slow dread on a crew vividly. He admits he would stay for the pay until the end, which sits alongside his push for retraining money for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly. Proper retraining, proper pensions, nobody left on the scrap heap. That's the line I'd take at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to start again, I suppose, though I can't picture doing anything else. Ten years means I'd get to be a proper driver before I'm an ex-driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving and keep my head down for the first few years. Stay on the union committee, push for a transition fund. Probably nothing big in the first year, to be honest, I'd wait and see if it's really coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Still a worry, but it's a far-off worry, not a this-Christmas worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. When would you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they start building the control room, I think. That's the sign. If I saw concrete going in for a remote centre, I'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to do something, and I don't know what. Mel says I'd be good with people, maybe something in health like her. I laughed at her, but I've thought about it since.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, with real retraining, real pensions and nobody left on the scrap heap. That's the line I'd take at work.
S4.think: Privately I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to start again, though I can't picture any other work. At least I'd get to be a proper driver first.
S4.do: Keeps driving and stays on the union committee pushing for a transition fund. Waits to see whether it's really coming, with a building of a remote control room as his signal to act.
S4.feel: Easier, a distant worry rather than an urgent one.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'd get to be a proper driver before I'm an ex-driver.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his worry drops a lot, and he names a concrete trigger for when he'd stop waiting. He brushed off his partner's suggestion of health work, then admitted he'd thought about it. That small crack is the only time he imagined a different job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. What would help is a guarantee, in writing, that the company can't just dump us. Keep paying us for a while, pay for retraining, and let the union have a say in when the trucks come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If Red Hill goes driverless, it's not just us drivers, it's the bakery, the football club, the bus driver. Everyone here lives off the pit one way or another.

headlineQuote: If Red Hill goes driverless, it's not just us drivers, it's the bakery, the football club, the bus driver.
portrait: Liam Jensen is 27, a second-year haul truck driver at the Red Hill copper pit who still has a trainer riding with him on some shifts. He lives with his partner Mel, a pharmacy worker, and has about three months of savings. He avoids new technology and puts his faith in the union, blaming owners and shareholders rather than the machines. He was uneasy even in the plateau picture because driverless trucks are coming regardless, alarmed by both fast AGI timelines, and noticeably calmer with ten years, though he still can't picture what else he'd do.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he thinks he'd be out of mining within a year with nothing he could retrain into.
whatWouldHelp: A written guarantee that the company keeps paying workers for a while, funds retraining and gives the union a say in when driverless trucks arrive.
